title: Numerical
notes: Stoichiometry is the math behind chemistry that allows us to calculate the exact quantities of reactants and products in a chemical reaction.
Word Origin: Derived from the Greek words stoicheion (element) and metron (measure).
Definition: It is the quantitative relationship between the substances that change during a chemical reaction.
Core Rule: It relies completely on the Law of Conservation of Mass — no atoms are created or destroyed during a reaction.
To Avoid Waste: It tells scientists exactly how much of each ingredient to mix so nothing is left over.
To Save Money: In chemical factories, using precise amounts avoids wasting expensive raw materials.
To Predict Outputs: It allows us to calculate exactly how much product (like a medicine or plastic) a reaction will yield before we even start.
To Ensure Safety: Knowing the exact amount of gas or heat produced keeps chemical reactions safe from explosions.
Balance Equations: We count and match atoms on both sides of a chemical reaction.
Convert Units: We change grams into moles, and moles into volumes or molecules.
Find Limiters: We identify the limiting reactant that will run out first and stop the reaction.
Calculate Yields: We determine the maximum possible amount of product we can theoretically create.
Stoichiometry is built on five distinct laws:
Core Rule: Total mass of reactants = Total mass of products.
$$w_1 + w_2 = w_3 + w_4 \quad (\text{where } w \text{ is mass in grams})$$
Apparatus: An H-shaped glass tube called Landolt's tube.
Chemicals used: Silver Nitrate ($AgNO_3$) and Sodium Chloride ($NaCl$).
Conclusion: The total weight of the tube remains exactly the same before and after the chemical reaction.
Statement: When gases react, they do so in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio to each other and to the gaseous products, provided temperature and pressure remain constant.
Only for Gases: This law applies strictly to reactants and products that are in the gaseous state (g).
Volume as "Moles": Instead of counting molecules or grams, you can directly use volumes (litres, mL, or cc) to relate reactants and products, as long as temperature and pressure do not change.
Simple Ratios: The relationship between these volumes is always in simple integers (like 1:1:2 or 2:1:2).
Illustration — reaction between hydrogen and chlorine gas:
1 volume of $H_2$ + 1 volume of $Cl_2$ → 2 volumes of $HCl$, a ratio of 1:1:2.
Problem: A 350 cc mixture of carbon monoxide (CO) and hydrogen ($H_2$) is completely burned with excess oxygen. It produces 200 cc of $CO_2$. Find the percentage of CO in the original mixture.
Reaction: Burning CO produces $CO_2$: $2CO(g) + O_2(g) \rightarrow 2CO_2(g)$, so 1 vol CO gives 1 vol $CO_2$.
Reasoning: Since 1 cc of CO makes 1 cc of $CO_2$, the 200 cc of $CO_2$ must have come from exactly 200 cc of CO.
